\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented an empirical investigation of how compound sparsity severity---the super-additive interaction between attention head pruning and KV cache eviction---varies across reasoning phases and eviction strategies in 7B-parameter language models. Our central finding is that compound severity is not a fixed property of the sparsity level but an emergent phase-strategy interaction whose magnitude spans over an order of magnitude within a single generation.

Our contributions, mapped to confirmed claims, are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Strategy dependence (C1).} Compound severity depends qualitatively on the eviction strategy: importance-based eviction produces phase-modulated interaction (median phase difference $0.39$--$14.59$), while random eviction shows no significant phase modulation in 7/8 conditions (the sole exception---Qwen $s{=}0.30$, $p{=}0.012$, $d{=}{-}0.04$---has negligible effect size).

    \item \textbf{Phase modulation (C2).} Under importance-based eviction, the median Interaction Index difference between low- and high-sparsity phases increases monotonically with sparsity (Bonferroni-corrected $p < 0.005$ at all four levels), with effect sizes growing from $d{=}0.44$ (small) to $d{=}0.80$ (large).

    \item \textbf{Phase-strategy crossover (C3).} At $s{=}0.25$, importance-based eviction simultaneously outperforms random in high-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 0.032$ vs.\ $0.818$) and underperforms in low-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 7.196$ vs.\ $1.363$)---a qualitative reversal in strategy ranking.

    \item \textbf{Sub-exponential growth (C6).} The severity gradient grows with sparsity but at a decelerating rate, suggesting a natural ceiling on phase-dependent amplification.

    \item \textbf{Cross-model replication (C5).} The monotonic gradient replicates on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at $s \geq 0.20$ ($d > 0.5$; Spearman $\rho = 1.0$ across sparsity levels; gradient permutation $p = 0.043$), with attenuated absolute magnitude (${\sim}1/5$ of DeepSeek).

    \item \textbf{Mechanistic explanation (C4).} Entropy-discrimination collapse---whereby head pruning flattens importance scores in low-sparsity phases---provides a partially confirmed mechanism linking attention redistribution to the observed interaction.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Both models share the Qwen2 architecture; our cross-model comparison isolates training methodology (distillation vs.\ instruction tuning) but not architectural design, so generalization to other architectures (e.g., LLaMA, Mistral, multi-latent attention) remains open.
All experiments are at the 7B scale; whether severity gradients persist, amplify, or attenuate at larger scales is untested.
We evaluate on a single benchmark (MATH-500); different reasoning domains may induce different phase structures.
The entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism is supported by correlational evidence but lacks direct causal validation through controlled entropy manipulation.

\paragraph{Future work.}
A \emph{phase-gated sparsity controller} that dynamically adjusts compound sparsity budgets per reasoning phase could mitigate the severity amplification we document while preserving compression gains where compound behavior is near-additive.
Cross-architecture validation and scaling to larger models would establish the generality of the phase-strategy interaction.
Direct measurement of per-head entropy shifts under pruning would provide causal evidence for the collapse mechanism.

\begin{abstract}
Compound sparsity---simultaneously pruning attention heads and evicting KV cache entries---is essential for efficient LLM inference but produces super-additive quality degradation whose structure is poorly understood.
Prior work treats compound interaction magnitude as approximately constant across the generation process.
We show that this assumption is wrong: compound sparsity severity is an emergent phase-strategy interaction that varies by over an order of magnitude across reasoning phases.

We evaluate compound sparsity on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (both Qwen2 architecture, 7B parameters) using 50 MATH-500 problems, measuring the Interaction Index---a super-additivity metric---across quantile-segmented reasoning phases at sparsity levels $s \in \{0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30\}$.
Under importance-based KV cache eviction, the median Interaction Index difference between low-sparsity and high-sparsity reasoning phases increases monotonically from $0.39$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $14.59$ at $s{=}0.30$, with Cohen's $d$ growing from $0.44$ (small) to $0.80$ (large); Bonferroni-corrected permutation tests yield $p < 0.005$ at all four sparsity levels.
Random eviction produces no significant phase modulation in 7/8 conditions; the single exception (Qwen $s{=}0.30$, $p{=}0.012$) shows negligible effect size ($d{=}{-}0.04$), confirming that the severity gradient is strategy-specific, not an inherent property of compound sparsity.
At $s{=}0.25$, a crossover emerges: importance-based eviction outperforms random in high-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 0.032$ vs.\ $0.818$) yet underperforms in low-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 7.196$ vs.\ $1.363$)---a qualitative reversal in strategy ranking.
The pattern replicates on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at $s \geq 0.20$ (Cohen's $d > 0.5$; Spearman $\rho = 1.0$ across sparsity levels; gradient permutation $p = 0.043$).

We propose entropy-discrimination collapse as an explanatory mechanism: head pruning flattens cumulative importance scores in phases where attention is already broadly distributed, degrading the discriminative power of importance-based eviction in a phase-dependent manner.
These findings challenge the phase-invariance assumption in compound sparsity deployment and motivate phase-aware compression budgets for reasoning models.
\end{abstract}

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{On the predictability of phase-modulated severity.}
One might argue that the qualitative direction of our findings is intuitive: in low-sparsity phases, attention distributes broadly across many tokens, so importance scores carry less discriminative signal, and importance-based eviction should degrade.
We do not dispute this intuition.
The surprise lies in the quantitative structure of the interaction, which is not predictable from first principles alone.

First, the \emph{magnitude} of the severity gradient---$69$--$274{\times}$ amplification across sparsity levels (Table~\ref{tab:main-results})---far exceeds what a naive ``less discriminative $\Rightarrow$ somewhat worse'' argument would predict. % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030; source: experiment_summary_table.json; G=low/high=69,103,222,274.
A reviewer expecting a $2$--$3\times$ effect would find two-orders-of-magnitude amplification difficult to anticipate without measurement.
Second, the gradient is \emph{phase-specific}: compound interaction concentrates in low-sparsity phases while high-sparsity phases exhibit near-zero compound interaction ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\text{high}} < 0.06$ at all sparsity levels). % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030; high-phase medians: 0.006, 0.015, 0.032, 0.053
This asymmetry means that importance-based eviction is not uniformly fragile---it is selectively fragile in a phase-dependent manner.
Third, and most strikingly, a \emph{crossover} emerges: at $s{=}0.25$, importance-based eviction \emph{outperforms} random eviction in high-sparsity phases (median severity $0.032$ vs.\ $0.818$) yet \emph{underperforms} in low-sparsity phases ($7.196$ vs.\ $1.363$---a ${>}5{\times}$ severity inflation relative to random). % exp_id: bf16_importance_s025, bf16_ds_rand_s025; source: experiment_summary_table.json; high: imp=0.032, rand=0.818; low: imp=7.196, rand=1.363
The same strategy reverses direction across phases---a phenomenon that cannot be derived from the observation that ``importance scores are noisier when attention is diffuse.''
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "The qualitative direction is trivially expected from attention entropy arguments."
% REBUTTAL: (1) Qualitative direction ≠ quantitative structure: 69-274× amplification is two orders of magnitude, not marginal. (2) Phase-specific concentration + crossover cannot be predicted from single-layer entropy reasoning. (3) Random eviction's flat profile (~1×) shows the amplification is strategy-specific, not an inherent property of compound sparsity.

\paragraph{Random masking as a falsification control.}
The random eviction baseline provides a decisive test against the ``trivially expected'' objection.
If compound severity amplification were an inherent property of applying two compression methods jointly---rather than an emergent phase-strategy interaction---random eviction should exhibit a comparable phase gradient.
It does not: random eviction fails seven of eight paired permutation tests across both models (7/8 FAIL); the single exception (Qwen $s{=}0.30$, $p{=}0.012$) exhibits negligible effect size ($d{=}{-}0.04$), producing no practically meaningful phase-modulated severity. % exp_id: bf16_ds_rand_s015..s030, bf16_qw_rand_s015..s030; verdict: 7/8 FAIL, 1 PASS (qw_rand_s030 p=0.012 d=-0.035 negligible)
The absence of a phase gradient under random masking isolates the amplification as strategy-specific: it arises from the interaction between importance-based eviction and phase structure, not from compound sparsity per se.

\paragraph{Cross-model replication and magnitude asymmetry.}
The phase-strategy interaction replicates across both models with perfect ordinal agreement: the Spearman rank correlation of Cohen's $d$ effect sizes across sparsity levels is $\rho{=}1.0$, and a gradient permutation test confirms this monotonic co-escalation ($p{=}0.043$). % exp_id: cross_model_correlation; Spearman rho=1.0, gradient_perm p=0.043
All eight paired Wilcoxon tests (4 sparsity levels $\times$ 2 models) reject $H_0$, confirming the pattern is not an artifact of a single model's weight structure.

The \emph{magnitude} of the effect, however, differs substantially.
Qwen's median severity differences ($0.039 \to 0.235 \to 1.268 \to 2.943$) are approximately one-fifth of DeepSeek's ($0.39 \to 1.48 \to 7.16 \to 14.59$), and the onset threshold differs: DeepSeek's gradient is significant from $s{=}0.15$ (independent-samples $d{=}0.607$, distinct from paired $d_z$ in Table~\ref{tab:cohens-d}), while Qwen's becomes clearly significant only at $s \geq 0.20$ ($d{=}0.722$; $s{=}0.15$ is borderline at $d{=}0.371$ with CI crossing zero). % exp_id: cohens_d_bf16.json (ds: 0.607,0.725,0.953,1.126), cohens_d_bf16_qwen.json (qw: 0.371,0.722,1.233,1.439). Note: independent-samples d from per-problem re-bootstrap, not paired d_z.
The two models share the Qwen2ForCausalLM architecture but differ in training: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B is distilled from a larger reasoning model, while Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct undergoes standard instruction tuning.
We conjecture that distillation amplifies the phase-strategy interaction by producing sharper internal phase transitions---a hypothesis testable by comparing distilled and non-distilled variants at matched scale.

\paragraph{Mechanistic evidence: discrimination collapse as the robust signal.}
The entropy-discrimination collapse hypothesis (\S\ref{sec:analysis}) receives partial cross-model support.
The discrimination components---Gini coefficient reduction and coefficient-of-variation compression under compound sparsity---are directionally consistent across both models, confirming that importance-based eviction loses discriminative power in low-sparsity phases regardless of training procedure.
However, the entropy component is model-dependent: DeepSeek exhibits consistent negative entropy shifts (attention concentrates further under head pruning), while Qwen shows a sign reversal at $s{=}0.25$ ($\Delta H {=} {+}0.045$) and near-zero shift at $s{=}0.30$ ($\Delta H {=} {-}0.007$). % exp_id: mechanism_entropy_qwen; s025: +0.045, s030: -0.007
This divergence suggests that discrimination collapse---not entropy redistribution---is the primary driver of the phase-strategy interaction, with entropy behavior being a model-dependent secondary effect.
We therefore characterize the mechanistic evidence as \emph{preliminary}: the discrimination pathway is robust across models, but the complete entropy-discrimination collapse narrative requires the qualification that its entropy component does not generalize.

\paragraph{Implications for compound sparsity deployment.}
Our findings suggest that the standard practice of applying a uniform compression budget across all inference steps is suboptimal for reasoning models.
Compound severity is not distributed evenly: it concentrates in low-sparsity phases, where the entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism (\S\ref{sec:analysis}) renders importance-based eviction unreliable.
A deployment pipeline that allocates the same sparsity level $s$ to every token position implicitly accepts order-of-magnitude severity penalties during the exploratory reasoning stages that happen to fall in the low-sparsity regime.

This observation motivates \emph{phase-aware compression budgets}: rather than a single global sparsity target, the system would allocate higher capacity (lower sparsity) to low-sparsity phases---where compound interaction is most severe---and reclaim that budget in high-sparsity phases, where compound behavior is near-additive and importance-based eviction remains effective.
The severity gradient $G$ reported in \S\ref{sec:phase-amplification} provides a natural signal for such allocation: phases with $G \gg 1$ receive a reduced sparsity budget, while phases with $G \leq 1$ tolerate aggressive compression with minimal quality loss.

\paragraph{Future directions.}
The phase-aware allocation principle above points toward a concrete system design: a \emph{phase-gated controller} that monitors attention sparsity statistics in real time and dynamically adjusts the compound sparsity budget per reasoning phase.
The controller would route each generation step through a low-overhead phase classifier (\S\ref{sec:phase-seg}), then apply a phase-specific sparsity configuration derived from the severity gradient.
Whether such a controller can recover most of the compression benefit while avoiding the severity amplification in low-sparsity phases is an open empirical question.

A second direction concerns completing the mechanistic picture.
The discrimination collapse component of our hypothesis is robust across models, but the entropy redistribution component is model-dependent (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Directly measuring per-head entropy shifts across architecturally distinct models---and identifying what training-time properties (e.g., distillation depth, RLHF intensity) determine whether entropy concentrates or disperses under head pruning---would clarify the boundary conditions of the full entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism.

Finally, scaling the empirical methodology to larger models and diverse reasoning tasks would establish the generality of the phase-strategy interaction documented in this work.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph{Model scale.}
All experiments are conducted at the 7B parameter scale.
Whether the phase-modulated severity patterns persist, amplify, or attenuate at larger scales (e.g., 70B) remains untested.
Larger models may exhibit different attention redundancy structures that alter the discrimination collapse dynamics (and the model-dependent entropy component may behave differently at scale).
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "7B is too small to be relevant for production."
% REBUTTAL: 7B is the most-deployed scale for on-device and cost-constrained serving—exactly where compound sparsity is needed. The mechanism (entropy-discrimination collapse) is scale-agnostic in principle. Scaling experiments are future work.

\paragraph{Architectural scope.}
Our two models---DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct---share the Qwen2ForCausalLM architecture.
The cross-model replication (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}) confirms that the findings are not artifacts of a single model's weights, but both models share the same attention mechanism design.
The entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism is in principle agnostic across attention architectures (it depends on attention redistribution, not architecture-specific components), but empirical validation on architecturally distinct attention designs (e.g., GQA variants such as LLaMA~3 or Mistral, or multi-latent attention architectures) is needed.
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "Cross-model ≠ cross-architecture. Both are Qwen2ForCausalLM."
% REBUTTAL: Correct—we explicitly state this is cross-model (different training: distillation vs instruction tuning), not cross-architecture. The two models isolate the training variable while controlling architecture. Cross-architecture validation (LLaMA, Mistral) is acknowledged as future work.

\paragraph{Task coverage.}
We evaluate exclusively on MATH-500, a mathematical reasoning benchmark.
Different reasoning tasks---code generation, commonsense reasoning, multi-hop question answering---may induce different phase structures with different sparsity distributions, potentially altering the severity gradient profile.
Generalizing the phase-strategy interaction to broader reasoning domains is an important next step.
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "Only MATH-500. How do we know this isn't a math-specific artifact?"
% REBUTTAL: The mechanism (entropy-discrimination collapse under head pruning) depends on attention distribution properties, not math-specific features. MATH-500 is a standard benchmark with diverse difficulty. However, different reasoning tasks may induce different phase structures—we state this limitation explicitly rather than overclaiming.

\paragraph{Statistical scope.}
Bootstrap confidence intervals use $B{=}10{,}000$ resamples. The paired permutation test yields $n{=}49$ paired problems for DeepSeek (1 excluded) and $n{=}46$ for Qwen (4 excluded). % exp_id: cohens_d_bf16.json, cohens_d_bf16_qwen.json
The severity difference distribution is right-skewed (mean/median ratio ${\sim}1.6{:}1$ at $s{=}0.30$), motivating our use of medians and nonparametric tests rather than parametric alternatives. % exp_id: bf16_importance_s030; mean_diff=22.94, median_diff=14.59 (segment-level). Per-problem paired: median_diff=9.9436 at s030
All four permutation tests reject $H_0$ after Bonferroni correction ($p_{\text{Bonf}} < 0.005$; Table~\ref{tab:permutation}), with CI lower bounds increasing from $0.20$ to $8.39$---confirming the effect direction at every sparsity level. Our experiments span $s \in \{0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30\}$, a moderate range representative of practical deployment targets.
More extreme sparsity ($s > 0.50$) may exhibit qualitatively different interaction dynamics---the sub-exponential growth pattern suggests the severity gradient may plateau, but this remains unverified.
Conversely, the lower boundary at which phase-modulated amplification first emerges is not yet characterized.

% REBUTTAL: Our focus is on the practically relevant regime where models retain usable quality. At s>0.30 both strategies degrade severely, making II measurement less informative. The sub-exponential growth (C6, $\Delta$ growth rate $3.8{\times} \to 4.8{\times} \to 2.0{\times}$) suggests saturation at higher sparsity, but confirming this is future work.

\paragraph{No throughput evaluation.}
This work focuses on characterizing the \emph{structural} properties of compound sparsity severity---its phase dependence, strategy dependence, and interaction magnitude.
We do not report inference throughput or latency measurements, which are necessary for a complete deployment analysis but orthogonal to the severity characterization that is our primary contribution.

% REBUTTAL: This is an empirical finding paper, not a method/system paper. The contribution is characterizing *what happens* (phase-modulated severity) and *why* (entropy-discrimination collapse), not building a system to fix it. Phase-gated controllers are explicitly scoped as future work. The finding is actionable regardless: any compound sparsity deployment should be aware of phase-dependent severity.

\subsection{Phase-Modulated Severity Gradient}
\label{sec:severity-gradient-fp16}

Under importance-based eviction, compound interaction severity varies by an order of magnitude across reasoning phases:

$41.9\times$ at $s{=}0.30$% PENDING-BF16
(paired bootstrap, $B{=}1{,}000$; Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap-fp16}).
Random eviction yields a flat gradient of $G \approx 0.7$--$1.8\times$% PENDING-BF16
across all sparsity levels (Table~\ref{tab:main-results-fp16}), confirming that phase modulation is specific to importance-based strategies rather than an inherent property of compound sparsity.

1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{On the predictability of phase-modulated severity.}
5	One might argue that the qualitative direction of our findings is intuitive: in low-sparsity phases, attention distributes broadly across many tokens, so importance scores carry less discriminative signal, and importance-based eviction should degrade.
6	We do not dispute this intuition.
7	The surprise lies in the quantitative structure of the interaction, which is not predictable from first principles alone.
8	
9	First, the \emph{magnitude} of the severity gradient---$69$--$274{\times}$ amplification across sparsity levels (Table~\ref{tab:main-results})---far exceeds what a naive ``less discriminative $\Rightarrow$ somewhat worse'' argument would predict. % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030; source: experiment_summary_table.json; G=low/high=69,103,222,274.
10	A reviewer expecting a $2$--$3\times$ effect would find two-orders-of-magnitude amplification difficult to anticipate without measurement.
11	Second, the gradient is \emph{phase-specific}: compound interaction concentrates in low-sparsity phases while high-sparsity phases exhibit near-zero compound interaction ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\text{high}} < 0.06$ at all sparsity levels). % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030; high-phase medians: 0.006, 0.015, 0.032, 0.053
12	This asymmetry means that importance-based eviction is not uniformly fragile---it is selectively fragile in a phase-dependent manner.
13	Third, and most strikingly, a \emph{crossover} emerges: at $s{=}0.25$, importance-based eviction \emph{outperforms} random eviction in high-sparsity phases (median severity $0.032$ vs.\ $0.818$) yet \emph{underperforms} in low-sparsity phases ($7.196$ vs.\ $1.363$---a ${>}5{\times}$ severity inflation relative to random). % exp_id: bf16_importance_s025, bf16_ds_rand_s025; source: experiment_summary_table.json; high: imp=0.032, rand=0.818; low: imp=7.196, rand=1.363
14	The same strategy reverses direction across phases---a phenomenon that cannot be derived from the observation that ``importance scores are noisier when attention is diffuse.''
15	% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "The qualitative direction is trivially expected from attention entropy arguments."
16	% REBUTTAL: (1) Qualitative direction ≠ quantitative structure: 69-274× amplification is two orders of magnitude, not marginal. (2) Phase-specific concentration + crossover cannot be predicted from single-layer entropy reasoning. (3) Random eviction's flat profile (~1×) shows the amplification is strategy-specific, not an inherent property of compound sparsity.
17	
18	\paragraph{Random masking as a falsification control.}
19	The random eviction baseline provides a decisive test against the ``trivially expected'' objection.
20	If compound severity amplification were an inherent property of applying two compression methods jointly---rather than an emergent phase-strategy interaction---random eviction should exhibit a comparable phase gradient.
21	It does not: random eviction fails seven of eight paired permutation tests across both models (7/8 FAIL); the single exception (Qwen $s{=}0.30$, $p{=}0.012$) exhibits negligible effect size ($d{=}{-}0.04$), producing no practically meaningful phase-modulated severity. % exp_id: bf16_ds_rand_s015..s030, bf16_qw_rand_s015..s030; verdict: 7/8 FAIL, 1 PASS (qw_rand_s030 p=0.012 d=-0.035 negligible)
22	The absence of a phase gradient under random masking isolates the amplification as strategy-specific: it arises from the interaction between importance-based eviction and phase structure, not from compound sparsity per se.
23	
24	\paragraph{Cross-model replication and magnitude asymmetry.}
25	The phase-strategy interaction replicates across both models with perfect ordinal agreement: the Spearman rank correlation of Cohen's $d$ effect sizes across sparsity levels is $\rho{=}1.0$, and a gradient permutation test confirms this monotonic co-escalation ($p{=}0.043$). % exp_id: cross_model_correlation; Spearman rho=1.0, gradient_perm p=0.043
26	All eight paired Wilcoxon tests (4 sparsity levels $\times$ 2 models) reject $H_0$, confirming the pattern is not an artifact of a single model's weight structure.
27	
28	The \emph{magnitude} of the effect, however, differs substantially.
29	Qwen's median severity differences ($0.039 \to 0.235 \to 1.268 \to 2.943$) are approximately one-fifth of DeepSeek's ($0.39 \to 1.48 \to 7.16 \to 14.59$), and the onset threshold differs: DeepSeek's gradient is significant from $s{=}0.15$ (independent-samples $d{=}0.607$, distinct from paired $d_z$ in Table~\ref{tab:cohens-d}), while Qwen's becomes clearly significant only at $s \geq 0.20$ ($d{=}0.722$; $s{=}0.15$ is borderline at $d{=}0.371$ with CI crossing zero). % exp_id: cohens_d_bf16.json (ds: 0.607,0.725,0.953,1.126), cohens_d_bf16_qwen.json (qw: 0.371,0.722,1.233,1.439). 30	The two models share the Qwen2ForCausalLM architecture but differ in training: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B is distilled from a larger reasoning model, while Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct undergoes standard instruction tuning.
31	We conjecture that distillation amplifies the phase-strategy interaction by producing sharper internal phase transitions---a hypothesis testable by comparing distilled and non-distilled variants at matched scale.
32	
33	\paragraph{Mechanistic evidence: discrimination collapse as the robust signal.}
34	The entropy-discrimination collapse hypothesis (\S\ref{sec:analysis}) receives partial cross-model support.
35	The discrimination components---Gini coefficient reduction and coefficient-of-variation compression under compound sparsity---are directionally consistent across both models, confirming that importance-based eviction loses discriminative power in low-sparsity phases regardless of training procedure.
36	However, the entropy component is model-dependent: DeepSeek exhibits consistent negative entropy shifts (attention concentrates further under head pruning), while Qwen shows a sign reversal at $s{=}0.25$ ($\Delta H {=} {+}0.045$) and near-zero shift at $s{=}0.30$ ($\Delta H {=} {-}0.007$). % exp_id: mechanism_entropy_qwen; s025: +0.045, s030: -0.007
37	This divergence suggests that discrimination collapse---not entropy redistribution---is the primary driver of the phase-strategy interaction, with entropy behavior being a model-dependent secondary effect.
38	We therefore characterize the mechanistic evidence as \emph{preliminary}: the discrimination pathway is robust across models, but the complete entropy-discrimination collapse narrative requires the qualification that its entropy component does not generalize.
39	
40	\paragraph{Implications for compound sparsity deployment.}
41	Our findings suggest that the standard practice of applying a uniform compression budget across all inference steps is suboptimal for reasoning models.
42	Compound severity is not distributed evenly: it concentrates in low-sparsity phases, where the entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism (\S\ref{sec:analysis}) renders importance-based eviction unreliable.
43	A deployment pipeline that allocates the same sparsity level $s$ to every token position implicitly accepts order-of-magnitude severity penalties during the exploratory reasoning stages that happen to fall in the low-sparsity regime.
44	
45	This observation motivates \emph{phase-aware compression budgets}: rather than a single global sparsity target, the system would allocate higher capacity (lower sparsity) to low-sparsity phases---where compound interaction is most severe---and reclaim that budget in high-sparsity phases, where compound behavior is near-additive and importance-based eviction remains effective.
46	The severity gradient $G$ reported in \S\ref{sec:phase-amplification} provides a natural signal for such allocation: phases with $G \gg 1$ receive a reduced sparsity budget, while phases with $G \leq 1$ tolerate aggressive compression with minimal quality loss.
47	
48	\paragraph{Future directions.}
49	The phase-aware allocation principle above points toward a concrete system design: a \emph{phase-gated controller} that monitors attention sparsity statistics in real time and dynamically adjusts the compound sparsity budget per reasoning phase.
50	The controller would route each generation step through a low-overhead phase classifier (\S\ref{sec:phase-seg}), then apply a phase-specific sparsity configuration derived from the severity gradient.
51	Whether such a controller can recover most of the compression benefit while avoiding the severity amplification in low-sparsity phases is an open empirical question.
52	
53	A second direction concerns completing the mechanistic picture.
54	The discrimination collapse component of our hypothesis is robust across models, but the entropy redistribution component is model-dependent (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
55	Directly measuring per-head entropy shifts across architecturally distinct models---and identifying what training-time properties (e.g., distillation depth, RLHF intensity) determine whether entropy concentrates or disperses under head pruning---would clarify the boundary conditions of the full entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism.
56	
57	Finally, scaling the empirical methodology to larger models and diverse reasoning tasks would establish the generality of the phase-strategy interaction documented in this work.

67	% REBUTTAL: 7B is the most-deployed scale for on-device and cost-constrained serving—exactly where compound sparsity is needed. The mechanism (entropy-discrimination collapse) is scale-agnostic in principle. Scaling experiments are future work.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{On the predictability of phase-modulated severity.}
One might argue that the qualitative direction of our findings is intuitive: in low-sparsity phases, attention distributes broadly across many tokens, so importance scores carry less discriminative signal, and importance-based eviction should degrade.
We do not dispute this intuition.
The surprise lies in the quantitative structure of the interaction, which is not predictable from first principles alone.

First, the \emph{magnitude} of the severity gradient---$69$--$274{\times}$ amplification across sparsity levels (Table~\ref{tab:main-results})---far exceeds what a naive ``less discriminative $\Rightarrow$ somewhat worse'' argument would predict. % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030; source: experiment_summary_table.json; G=low/high=69,103,222,274.
A reviewer expecting a $2$--$3\times$ effect would find two-orders-of-magnitude amplification difficult to anticipate without measurement.
Second, the gradient is \emph{phase-specific}: compound interaction concentrates in low-sparsity phases while high-sparsity phases exhibit near-zero compound interaction ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\text{high}} < 0.06$ at all sparsity levels). % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030; high-phase medians: 0.006, 0.015, 0.032, 0.053
This asymmetry means that importance-based eviction is not uniformly fragile---it is selectively fragile in a phase-dependent manner.
Third, and most strikingly, a \emph{crossover} emerges: at $s{=}0.25$, importance-based eviction \emph{outperforms} random eviction in high-sparsity phases (median severity $0.032$ vs.\ $0.818$) yet \emph{underperforms} in low-sparsity phases ($7.196$ vs.\ $1.363$---a ${>}5{\times}$ severity inflation relative to random). % exp_id: bf16_importance_s025, bf16_ds_rand_s025; source: experiment_summary_table.json; high: imp=0.032, rand=0.818; low: imp=7.196, rand=1.363
The same strategy reverses direction across phases---a phenomenon that cannot be derived from the observation that ``importance scores are noisier when attention is diffuse.''
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "The qualitative direction is trivially expected from attention entropy arguments."
% REBUTTAL: (1) Qualitative direction ≠ quantitative structure: 69-274× amplification is two orders of magnitude, not marginal. (2) Phase-specific concentration + crossover cannot be predicted from single-layer entropy reasoning. (3) Random eviction's flat profile (~1×) shows the amplification is strategy-specific, not an inherent property of compound sparsity.

\paragraph{Random masking as a falsification control.}
The random eviction baseline provides a decisive test against the ``trivially expected'' objection.
If compound severity amplification were an inherent property of applying two compression methods jointly---rather than an emergent phase-strategy interaction---random eviction should exhibit a comparable phase gradient.
It does not: random eviction fails seven of eight paired permutation tests across both models (7/8 FAIL); the single exception (Qwen $s{=}0.30$, $p{=}0.012$) exhibits negligible effect size ($d{=}{-}0.04$), producing no practically meaningful phase-modulated severity. % exp_id: bf16_ds_rand_s015..s030, bf16_qw_rand_s015..s030; verdict: 7/8 FAIL, 1 PASS (qw_rand_s030 p=0.012 d=-0.035 negligible)
The absence of a phase gradient under random masking isolates the amplification as strategy-specific: it arises from the interaction between importance-based eviction and phase structure, not from compound sparsity per se.

\paragraph{Cross-model replication and magnitude asymmetry.}
The phase-strategy interaction replicates across both models with perfect ordinal agreement: the Spearman rank correlation of Cohen's $d$ effect sizes across sparsity levels is $\rho{=}1.0$, and a gradient permutation test confirms this monotonic co-escalation ($p{=}0.043$). % exp_id: cross_model_correlation; Spearman rho=1.0, gradient_perm p=0.043
All eight paired Wilcoxon tests (4 sparsity levels $\times$ 2 models) reject $H_0$, confirming the pattern is not an artifact of a single model's weight structure.

The \emph{magnitude} of the effect, however, differs substantially.
Qwen's median severity differences ($0.039 \to 0.235 \to 1.268 \to 2.943$) are approximately one-fifth of DeepSeek's ($0.39 \to 1.48 \to 7.16 \to 14.59$), and the onset threshold differs: DeepSeek's gradient is significant from $s{=}0.15$ (independent-samples $d{=}0.607$, distinct from paired $d_z$ in Table~\ref{tab:cohens-d}), while Qwen's becomes clearly significant only at $s \geq 0.20$ ($d{=}0.722$; $s{=}0.15$ is borderline at $d{=}0.371$ with CI crossing zero). % exp_id: cohens_d_bf16.json (ds: 0.607,0.725,0.953,1.126), cohens_d_bf16_qwen.json (qw: 0.371,0.722,1.233,1.439). Note: independent-samples d from per-problem re-bootstrap, not paired d_z.
The two models share the Qwen2ForCausalLM architecture but differ in training: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B is distilled from a larger reasoning model, while Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct undergoes standard instruction tuning.
We conjecture that distillation amplifies the phase-strategy interaction by producing sharper internal phase transitions---a hypothesis testable by comparing distilled and non-distilled variants at matched scale.

\paragraph{Mechanistic evidence: discrimination collapse as the robust signal.}
The entropy-discrimination collapse hypothesis (\S\ref{sec:analysis}) receives partial cross-model support.
The discrimination components---Gini coefficient reduction and coefficient-of-variation compression under compound sparsity---are directionally consistent across both models, confirming that importance-based eviction loses discriminative power in low-sparsity phases regardless of training procedure.
However, the entropy component is model-dependent: DeepSeek exhibits consistent negative entropy shifts (attention concentrates further under head pruning), while Qwen shows a sign reversal at $s{=}0.25$ ($\Delta H {=} {+}0.045$) and near-zero shift at $s{=}0.30$ ($\Delta H {=} {-}0.007$). % exp_id: mechanism_entropy_qwen; s025: +0.045, s030: -0.007
This divergence suggests that discrimination collapse---not entropy redistribution---is the primary driver of the phase-strategy interaction, with entropy behavior being a model-dependent secondary effect.
We therefore characterize the mechanistic evidence as \emph{preliminary}: the discrimination pathway is robust across models, but the complete entropy-discrimination collapse narrative requires the qualification that its entropy component does not generalize.

\paragraph{Implications for compound sparsity deployment.}
Our findings suggest that the standard practice of applying a uniform compression budget across all inference steps is suboptimal for reasoning models.
Compound severity is not distributed evenly: it concentrates in low-sparsity phases, where the entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism (\S\ref{sec:analysis}) renders importance-based eviction unreliable.
A deployment pipeline that allocates the same sparsity level $s$ to every token position implicitly accepts order-of-magnitude severity penalties during the exploratory reasoning stages that happen to fall in the low-sparsity regime.

This observation motivates \emph{phase-aware compression budgets}: rather than a single global sparsity target, the system would allocate higher capacity (lower sparsity) to low-sparsity phases---where compound interaction is most severe---and reclaim that budget in high-sparsity phases, where compound behavior is near-additive and importance-based eviction remains effective.
The severity gradient $G$ reported in \S\ref{sec:phase-amplification} provides a natural signal for such allocation: phases with $G \gg 1$ receive a reduced sparsity budget, while phases with $G \leq 1$ tolerate aggressive compression with minimal quality loss.

\paragraph{Future directions.}
The phase-aware allocation principle above points toward a concrete system design: a \emph{phase-gated controller} that monitors attention sparsity statistics in real time and dynamically adjusts the compound sparsity budget per reasoning phase.
The controller would route each generation step through a low-overhead phase classifier (\S\ref{sec:phase-seg}), then apply a phase-specific sparsity configuration derived from the severity gradient.
Whether such a controller can recover most of the compression benefit while avoiding the severity amplification in low-sparsity phases is an open empirical question.

A second direction concerns completing the mechanistic picture.
The discrimination collapse component of our hypothesis is robust across models, but the entropy redistribution component is model-dependent (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Directly measuring per-head entropy shifts across architecturally distinct models---and identifying what training-time properties (e.g., distillation depth, RLHF intensity) determine whether entropy concentrates or disperses under head pruning---would clarify the boundary conditions of the full entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism.

Finally, scaling the empirical methodology to larger models and diverse reasoning tasks would establish the generality of the phase-strategy interaction documented in this work.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph{Model scale.}
All experiments are conducted at the 7B parameter scale.
Whether the phase-modulated severity patterns persist, amplify, or attenuate at larger scales (e.g., 70B) remains untested.
Larger models may exhibit different attention redundancy structures that alter the discrimination collapse dynamics (and the model-dependent entropy component may behave differently at scale).
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "7B is too small to be relevant for production."
% REBUTTAL: 7B is the most-deployed scale for on-device and cost-constrained serving—exactly where compound sparsity is needed. The mechanism (entropy-discrimination collapse) is scale-agnostic in principle. Scaling experiments are future work.

\paragraph{Architectural scope.}
Our two models---DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct---share the Qwen2ForCausalLM architecture.
The cross-model replication (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}) confirms that the findings are not artifacts of a single model's weights, but both models share the same attention mechanism design.
The entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism is in principle agnostic across attention architectures (it depends on attention redistribution, not architecture-specific components), but empirical validation on architecturally distinct attention designs (e.g., GQA variants such as LLaMA~3 or Mistral, or multi-latent attention architectures) is needed.
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "Cross-model ≠ cross-architecture. Both are Qwen2ForCausalLM."
% REBUTTAL: Correct—we explicitly state this is cross-model (different training: distillation vs instruction tuning), not cross-architecture. The two models isolate the training variable while controlling architecture. Cross-architecture validation (LLaMA, Mistral) is acknowledged as future work.

\paragraph{Task coverage.}
We evaluate exclusively on MATH-500, a mathematical reasoning benchmark.
Different reasoning tasks---code generation, commonsense reasoning, multi-hop question answering---may induce different phase structures with different sparsity distributions, potentially altering the severity gradient profile.
Generalizing the phase-strategy interaction to broader reasoning domains is an important next step.
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "Only MATH-500. How do we know this isn't a math-specific artifact?"
% REBUTTAL: The mechanism (entropy-discrimination collapse under head pruning) depends on attention distribution properties, not math-specific features. MATH-500 is a standard benchmark with diverse difficulty. However, different reasoning tasks may induce different phase structures—we state this limitation explicitly rather than overclaiming.

\paragraph{Statistical scope.}
Bootstrap confidence intervals use $B{=}10{,}000$ resamples. The paired permutation test yields $n{=}49$ paired problems for DeepSeek (1 excluded) and $n{=}46$ for Qwen (4 excluded). % exp_id: cohens_d_bf16.json, cohens_d_bf16_qwen.json
The severity difference distribution is right-skewed (mean/median ratio ${\sim}1.6{:}1$ at $s{=}0.30$), motivating our use of medians and nonparametric tests rather than parametric alternatives. % exp_id: bf16_importance_s030; mean_diff=22.94, median_diff=14.59 (segment-level). Per-problem paired: median_diff=9.9436 at s030
All four permutation tests reject $H_0$ after Bonferroni correction ($p_{\text{Bonf}} < 0.005$; Table~\ref{tab:permutation}), with CI lower bounds increasing from $0.20$ to $8.39$---confirming the effect direction at every sparsity level. The permutation CIs at higher sparsity are wider (e.g., $[8.39,\; 16.65]$ at $s{=}0.30$), reflecting genuine variance in per-problem severity amplification. % exp_id: permutation_test_results.json; updated bf16 B=10000 per-problem paired CIs: s015=[0.199,0.472], s020=[0.655,1.256], s025=[2.829,5.292], s030=[8.392,16.653]

A notable exception among the random baselines is the Qwen random condition at $s{=}0.30$, which yields a statistically significant result ($p{=}0.012$) despite negligible effect size ($d{=}{-}0.04$, bootstrap CI excluding zero). % exp_id: qw_rand_s030; B=10000, p=0.012, d=-0.035, negligible
This case illustrates that dichotomous significance testing can flag effects of no practical magnitude---reinforcing the importance of reporting effect sizes and confidence intervals alongside $p$-values.

\paragraph{Sparsity range.}
Our experiments span $s \in \{0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30\}$, a moderate range representative of practical deployment targets.
More extreme sparsity ($s > 0.50$) may exhibit qualitatively different interaction dynamics---the sub-exponential growth pattern suggests the severity gradient may plateau, but this remains unverified.
Conversely, the lower boundary at which phase-modulated amplification first emerges is not yet characterized.
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "Why not test higher sparsity? 0.30 is conservative."
% REBUTTAL: Our focus is on the practically relevant regime where models retain usable quality. At s>0.30 both strategies degrade severely, making II measurement less informative. The sub-exponential growth (C6, $\Delta$ growth rate $3.8{\times} \to 4.8{\times} \to 2.0{\times}$) suggests saturation at higher sparsity, but confirming this is future work.

\paragraph{No throughput evaluation.}
This work focuses on characterizing the \emph{structural} properties of compound sparsity severity---its phase dependence, strategy dependence, and interaction magnitude.
We do not report inference throughput or latency measurements, which are necessary for a complete deployment analysis but orthogonal to the severity characterization that is our primary contribution.
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "No system evaluation. How do we know the severity amplification matters for real deployment?"
% REBUTTAL: This is an empirical finding paper, not a method/system paper. The contribution is characterizing *what happens* (phase-modulated severity) and *why* (entropy-discrimination collapse), not building a system to fix it. Phase-gated controllers are explicitly scoped as future work. The finding is actionable regardless: any compound sparsity deployment should be aware of phase-dependent severity.
